clue.text: Service tuber in base after modifying radiation taken in (12, two words)

indicators.note: the service and tuber words sit inside the base word, so their letters go within it
the base word comes after being modified, so its letters are rearranged before anything goes into it

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged and opened up after its first two letters
the service tree is also called the sorb
an eddo is a taro tuber

explanation.surface: A gardener describes a tree and a root vegetable being grown at a modified base.
explanation.walkthrough: Service is not a church or tennis term here: it is the service tree, whose old name is sorb. The base is rearranged so that it splits two and two around the tree and tuber.
explanation.definitionFit: Absorbed dose is the physics term for the radiation energy a body or material actually takes up.

clue.text: Lout with locks uniformly cut in backwoods, ƒ

indicators.note: both words are cut in the same way, each losing its final letter

parts.note: a boor is a rude, uncouth person; its last letter goes
locks of hair; its last letter goes too

explanation.surface: A yokel with a ragged haircut out in the sticks, leading on to the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing mark links this clue to 3 down, which continues the yokel's story. Boohai is New Zealand slang: 'up the boohai' means out in the wilds.
explanation.definitionFit: In New Zealand usage the boohai is remote back-country, the equivalent of the backwoods or the sticks.

clue.text: ƒ His shock maybe suggesting one going rapidly downhill, we hear?

indicators.note: what we hear is the spoken form, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: someone skiing fast down a slope, said in casual speech

explanation.surface: Continuing 2 down, the yokel's wild hair looks like he has just raced down a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'His' is the backwoodsman of 2 down; his shock of hair is the tangle, like a coil of loose yarn.
explanation.definitionFit: A skein is a loose coil or tangle of thread, and a shock of hair is just such a tangled mass.

clue.text: Extravagance once shown by one in wild sortie

indicators.note: something wild is out of control, so the letters run riot into a new order

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A reckless military raid shows wasteful excess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks an obsolete word; 'in' is part of the anagram's wording, putting the I among the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Riotise is Spenser's word for riotous living or excess, an archaic equivalent of extravagance.

clue.text: Past name almost meaningless, no longer mentioned

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of it, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: gone by means past
N is the abbreviation for name
empty words are meaningless; the last letter goes

explanation.surface: An old name has become almost meaningless and nobody speaks of it now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' says the definition is archaic: it means mentioned or named, not forgotten as the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Bynempt is an obsolete past participle of bename, so it once meant named or mentioned.

clue.text: Hum was current in data transmission

indicators.note: the flowing verb goes inside the abbreviation, placing its letters within

parts.note: DT is the abbreviation for data transmission
a current runs, so was current is ran

explanation.surface: Electrical humming while current flowed through a data line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks electrical, matching the hum, but here it is the verb run in the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Drant is a Scots and dialect word meaning to drone or drawl, much like a monotonous hum.

clue.text: Jamaican nester? Grand one nesting in pipe

indicators.note: nesting inside something means sitting within it, so these letters go inside the pipe word

parts.note: a duct is a pipe or channel
a grand is a thousand, abbreviated K
an means one

explanation.surface: A Jamaican bird building its nest in a pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nester' suggests a bird, but this nester is an insect; the question mark warns of that.
explanation.definitionFit: The duck ant is a Jamaican termite that builds large nests in trees, so it is a nest-maker from Jamaica.

clue.text: Perfumed stuff in corded silk man peeled off

indicators.note: peeling something off removes it, so these letters are taken away from the silk

parts.note: ottoman is a heavy ribbed silk fabric
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: Scent sprayed on a silk garment that a man has taken off.
explanation.walkthrough: Ottoman, here a fabric rather than a footstool, loses MAN from its end.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto, also attar, is a fragrant essential oil pressed from rose petals and used in perfume.

clue.text: Sydney's beloved? It's out of order

definitions.text: Sydney's beloved? It's out of order

parts.note: surface reading: someone dear to the Australian city, or to a man called Sydney
setter's reading: the lady of Sir Philip Sidney's sonnets, a married woman whose courtship was improper, out of order

explanation.surface: A question about who Sydney loves, met with a rebuke that it is not proper to ask.
explanation.walkthrough: Sidney's sonnet sequence Astrophel and Stella addresses Penelope Rich, married to another man, so his love was out of order. The respelling as Sydney is part of the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Stella is the name Sir Philip Sidney gave the woman he loved and celebrated in his Elizabethan sonnet sequence.

clue.text: Extortioner enveloping food in sauce?

indicators.note: the sauce wraps around the food, so one word's letters go round the other's

parts.note: soya sauce, the Chinese condiment
kai is a New Zealand word for food

explanation.surface: Someone extorting money while wrapping food in a sauce, a strange culinary crime.
explanation.walkthrough: The Maori word for food is a Chambers favourite. 'Enveloping' says the sauce is wrapped round it, giving the Japanese word SOKAIYA.
explanation.definitionFit: Sokaiya are Japanese racketeers who extort companies by threatening to disrupt their shareholders' meetings.

clue.text: Mortified about pop, brother producing mushroom grower (10, two words)

indicators.note: about means going around, so the feeling word surrounds the others

parts.note: sick as in sick with embarrassment
to pop something is slang for pawning it
BR is the abbreviation for brother

explanation.surface: An embarrassed man whose father and brother turn out to grow mushrooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' and 'brother' look like a family, but pop is the slang verb meaning to hock something at a pawnshop.
explanation.definitionFit: A spawn brick is a compressed block of manure and mycelium from which cultivated mushrooms are grown.

clue.text: Sponger

parts.note: reading one: one who uses a sponge, as for washing
reading two: a scrounger who lives off other people's generosity

explanation.walkthrough: This is Azed's competition clue: the word is given by a bare definition and readers send in their own clues for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponger cadges from others without paying their share, which is exactly what a scrounger of free meals and lodging does.

clue.text: Rhymer, Old English in part

indicators.note: the old language is placed inside the part, so its letters go within

parts.note: PT is the standard abbreviation for part
OE is the usual abbreviation for Old English

explanation.surface: A verse-maker reading Old English in a part, as at a recital.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rhymes is a versifier, and poet is the general word for a writer of verse.

clue.text: Short piece for cast disguised by carotene

indicators.note: something disguised has its appearance altered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: the orange pigment in carrots

explanation.surface: An actor in a short play made up with carotene to look the part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like it belongs to the disguise, but it is the troupe of actors who perform the short play.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-acter is a play in a single act, a brief drama written for a cast of actors.

clue.text: After Scotch a woman'll have a dash of tonic

parts.note: taken as written
a dash of something is a small amount of it, a trace
surface only: what the woman will take with her whisky
surface only: says what the small amount is of

explanation.surface: After her whisky a woman will want just a splash of tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch' looks like the drink, but with 'After' it marks a Scots word for behind or after. 'A dash' is A HINT.
explanation.definitionFit: Ahint is the Scots adverb and preposition for behind or after, alongside ahind.

clue.text: Source of African beef? Love dividing joint

indicators.note: the love score splits the joint in two, so it is placed inside that word

parts.note: the joint between foot and leg
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A cut of meat from Africa, with romance coming between the joints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' dividing ANKLE gives ANK-O-LE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ankole cattle are a long-horned East African breed raised for beef and milk, so the breed is where that beef comes from.

clue.text: E.g. tide chart experienced sailor kept in hat

indicators.note: something kept in a hat is held inside it, so these letters go within the hat word

parts.note: tile is old slang for a hat
to have met something is to have experienced it
AB, able-bodied seaman, is the usual crossword sailor

explanation.surface: An old sea dog keeps the tide chart tucked inside his hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Tile is old slang for a hat, which a solver may not know; 'experienced' is the past tense of meet, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A tide table lists the times of high and low water, so it is an example of a schedule of times.

clue.text: Stench in bin if festering

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words, its letters running on across the gaps

parts.note: the letters run consecutively from the end of the first word into the third

explanation.surface: A foul smell coming from a dustbin left to rot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Festering' looks like an anagram signal but is part of the hiding place. Niff is British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Niff is an informal British word for an unpleasant odour, the same as a pong or stink.

clue.text: Scented bloom woven by faeries

indicators.note: weaving interlaces strands into a new pattern, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, in the old spelling

explanation.surface: A sweet-smelling flower woven into a garland by fairies.
explanation.definitionFit: Freesia is a South African plant of the iris family grown for its fragrant flowers.

clue.text: Silky material, last bit going in auction, last bit going

indicators.note: the first piece goes into the auction word, placing its letters inside
the final letter of the auction word departs before anything is inserted

parts.note: a sale by auction; its final letter is then removed
the end is the last bit of anything

explanation.surface: At an auction, the last lot of silky fabric is being sold off.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'last bit going' does two jobs: first a word for last bit goes into the auction word, then the auction word's own last letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sendal is a thin medieval silk fabric, used for fine garments and banners.

clue.text: Stitched edging round jumper? Pilot requires plenty of this (7, two words)

indicators.note: the edging goes round the jumper, surrounding its letters

parts.note: a seam is the stitched line where two edges are joined
a roo, short for kangaroo, is a jumper

explanation.surface: Knitting talk about a jumper's edging, then a pilot who needs lots of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' looks like a knitted pullover, which suits the stitching, but it is the kangaroo. The pilot is a ship's pilot, not a flyer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea room is open water clear of hazards in which a ship can manoeuvre safely, which a pilot needs.

clue.text: Grenade exploding — it warns opponent of coming attack (7, two words)

definitions.text: it warns opponent of coming attack

indicators.note: an explosion scatters the pieces, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bursting grenade alerts the enemy that an assault is imminent.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is military, but the attack is a fencer's.
explanation.definitionFit: En garde is the fencing call telling an opponent to take a guarding position before a bout begins.

clue.text: Clerical headgear indicating bishop before tribunal's judgement

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
an arrêt is the judgement or decree of a French court

explanation.surface: A bishop's cap signals the ruling of a church tribunal before it is announced.
explanation.definitionFit: A barret is a flat cap, and the word is used for the biretta worn by Roman Catholic clergy.

clue.text: Lost match, making Scots very cross

parts.note: Scots ae, literally one, also serves as an intensifier before superlatives
a mule is a cross between a donkey and a horse

explanation.surface: Scottish fans furious after their team lose a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost' signals an obsolete word, not a defeat, and 'match' is the verb to rival or equal. A mule is a hybrid, a cross.
explanation.definitionFit: Aemule is an obsolete Spenserian verb meaning to emulate or rival, and to match someone is to equal them.

clue.text: Everything in Spain is a shemozzle

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Spanish word for everything
second meaning: a muddle or commotion

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a complaint about Spain; the halves are a Spanish word and an English fuss word spelt the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Todo means all or everything in Spanish, and a to-do is a fuss or commotion, much like a shemozzle.

clue.text: Altar cloth ladies knitted that is cut round gold tincture

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round the heraldic colour, enclosing it
knitting loops yarn into a new form, so what remains is rearranged
cut means removed, so the letters of that is are taken out

parts.note: taken as written
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is
or is the heraldic tincture gold

explanation.surface: Women of the parish knit a cloth for the altar with gold thread.
explanation.walkthrough: The deletion comes first, leaving four letters to rearrange around the gold. 'Tincture' is the heraldic term for a colour or metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dorsal, also dossal, is an ornamental cloth hung behind an altar.

clue.text: Preach e.g. on conversion before life's end — it gives losers another chance

indicators.note: something converted is changed into a new form, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, with the abbreviation's letters included

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word life

explanation.surface: A sermon on religious conversion near death offers sinners a second chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conversion' and 'losers another chance' both fit a preacher's surface; the definition is a sporting term.
explanation.definitionFit: A repechage is an extra heat in rowing or cycling in which losers of earlier rounds get a second shot at qualifying.

clue.text: Ex-president driving off on rocky outcrop

indicators.note: driving something off sends it away, so these letters leave the name

parts.note: Bill Clinton, former US president
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: A former president driving away on rough rocky ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driving off on' reads as one motoring phrase, but on is the piece driven off.
explanation.definitionFit: Clint is a Scots and Northern English word for a hard rock or projecting ledge, as in limestone pavement.

clue.text: A weaver raised dust

indicators.note: in a down entry raising something lifts it to read bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
a loom is the machine that weaves

explanation.surface: A weaver at work stirring up dust from the threads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dust' is old slang for money, not powder.
explanation.definitionFit: Moola is slang for money, and dust has been slang for cash since the seventeenth century.

clue.text: Botched simple drives

indicators.note: a botched job is done badly, so the letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A golfer's easy shots off the tee have gone badly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drives' reads as golf shots, a noun, but the definition is the verb meaning pushes forward.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to push or urge forward, so impels is a synonym of drives as a verb.

clue.text: Page 3 of 25 — requirement for next day's lesson?

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for page
the first three letters of the answer to 25 across

explanation.surface: A schoolchild reading page three of a set text as homework.
explanation.walkthrough: '3 of 25' is not a page number but the opening three letters of the 25 across answer, REPECHAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Prep is British school slang for homework, done in preparation for the following day's lessons.

clue.text: A person circumventing rule, poet's gone astray

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to circumvent is literally to go around, so the person surrounds the rule

parts.note: bod is British slang for a person
R is the abbreviation for rule

explanation.surface: Someone dodging the rules has wandered off the straight and narrow.
explanation.walkthrough: In Azed, 'poet' usually means Spenser: the word is one of his archaisms.
explanation.definitionFit: Abord is a Spenserian adverb meaning astray or at a loss, so 'poet's' marks the poetic usage.

clue.text: Dogs with bread brought back for old tramp

parts.note: curs are mongrel dogs

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the bread word is read right to left

parts.note: roti is Indian flatbread, then turned round

explanation.surface: A down-and-out once shared his bread with stray dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: Cursitor is an obsolete word for a vagrant or wanderer, from Latin for a runner.

clue.text: What'll produce down, head laid to rest (i.e. Scottish down)?

indicators.note: laying a head to rest here means removing the first letter for good

parts.note: a goose grows the soft feathers used in pillows

explanation.surface: A sleepy question about pillow stuffing: where does down come from, once your head is resting on it?
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'down' is feathers, and the clue's head losing its rest is GOOSE losing G.
explanation.definitionFit: Oose is a Scots word for fluff or nap, the fine fuzz that gathers like down.

clue.text: Old rum drunk, one imbibed in standard units

indicators.note: what is imbibed is taken inside, so this letter goes within the others
someone drunk staggers about, so the letters lurch into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a means one, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: Old rum knocked back, with a drink taken in measured shots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old rum' reads as a vintage spirit but is simply six letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Modular construction is built from standardised components, the units that fit together interchangeably.

clue.text: Organ distention at my age? O help, that's wretched!

indicators.note: something wretched is in a miserable, broken state, so the preceding letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, every letter used

explanation.surface: An elderly patient groans about a swollen organ at their time of life.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a believable lament, and the fodder is all twelve letters of the plea.
explanation.definitionFit: Hepatomegaly is the medical term for an abnormally enlarged liver, the organ being swollen.
